prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement of the box office?
hint: It describes how well, not what.

choices.text: A customer can book a seat for any show that is currently on sale
choices.why: That is a behaviour: what the system does. It is functional.

choices.text: A booked seat cannot be booked a second time by another customer
choices.why: Also a behaviour, and a functional test already checks it with a 409.

choices.text: The booking answers within 500 ms while 200 people book at once
choices.why: Right. It says how well the booking behaves, under a stated load.

choices.text: The list of shows holds only the shows that are on sale
choices.why: A rule about what the list contains, so it is functional.

prompt: Why does a demonstration rarely reveal a non-functional defect?
hint: Think about who is using the system during a demo.

choices.text: Demonstrations run on a different version of the code
choices.why: Usually the same build; the difference is in the conditions, not the code.

choices.text: One friendly user, on a fast connection, looking at the screen
choices.why: Right. Load, assistive technology and hostile intent are all absent.

choices.text: Non-functional defects only appear after months in production
choices.why: A spike or a missing label shows up on the first day it meets the right user.

choices.text: The tools that find them cannot run during a demo
choices.why: Tools are not the issue; the demo simply never creates the conditions.

prompt: Match each third of the course to the question it asks.
hint: The table in the first reading section.

pairs.right: does it answer in time at the load it will meet?
can somebody use it with a keyboard and a screen reader?
does it refuse somebody trying on purpose?
does somebody find out first when it misbehaves?

right_distractors: does it do what the specification says?

prompt: What does a load test hand back where a functional test hands back pass or fail?
hint: Run the same request many times.

choices.text: Many timings, judged against a written threshold
choices.why: Right. Without the threshold the distribution decides nothing.

choices.text: A list of findings, each of which a person then has to rate
choices.why: That is closer to an accessibility audit or a security scan.

choices.text: A pass or a fail, exactly as the functional test gives
choices.why: Only once a threshold exists; the tool alone returns numbers.

choices.text: A single response time that stands for the whole system
choices.why: There is no single time: every request takes its own.

prompt: Which part is missing from "GET /shows/{id} answers in under 200 ms at the 95th percentile, timed at the client, for 10 minutes"?

choices.text: The operation
choices.why: It names GET /shows/{id}.

choices.text: The statistic
choices.why: The 95th percentile is there.

choices.text: The load
choices.why: Right. Nothing says how many requests a second, and at one user the sentence is easy to meet.

choices.text: The conditions
choices.why: Ten minutes, timed at the client: the conditions are stated.

prompt: Put the five parts of a performance requirement in the order the lesson gives them.
hint: From what is measured to where it is measured.

prompt: A team writes "the site must be fast" and runs a load test first, planning to set the threshold from the results. What goes wrong?
hint: Who decides what fail means, and when?

choices.text: The threshold ends up describing the system instead of judging it
choices.why: Right. A number chosen around the result can never fail that result.

choices.text: Load tests cannot run at all before a requirement has been written
choices.why: They run perfectly well; they just decide nothing.

choices.text: The results are too slow to arrive to be useful
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; the absence of a prior verdict is.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the threshold is written down eventually
choices.why: Writing it afterwards is exactly the mistake the lesson names.

prompt: Which statement is a testable accessibility requirement?
hint: Two readers must reach the same verdict.

choices.text: The booking flow must be accessible to all
choices.why: An adjective: nobody can say fail without asking what was meant.

choices.text: The booking flow conforms to WCAG 2.2 at level AA
choices.why: Right. A published, versioned list of criteria is something a test can fail.

choices.text: The booking page should be easy for everyone to use
choices.why: Easy for whom, measured how? Still a wish.

choices.text: Accessibility gets reviewed by the team before each release
choices.why: A process, not a property; it says nothing a result could fail.

prompt: Production logs show that, in the box office's peak minute today, 95 of every 100 requests answer under 140 ms. Which threshold for the next release has the strongest reason behind it?
hint: The first source of numbers in the lesson.

choices.text: Under 140 ms at the 95th percentile, at today's busiest minute
choices.why: Right. Keeping today's behaviour at today's load is a threshold nobody can call arbitrary.

choices.text: Average under 50 ms, because averages are easier to read
choices.why: The average is the wrong statistic, and 50 has no source.

choices.text: 95th percentile under 2.5 s, from Core Web Vitals
choices.why: 2.5 s is a front-end threshold for LCP, not an API's response time.

choices.text: Whatever the first load test against the release measures
choices.why: That writes the requirement around the result.

prompt: "The 95th percentile is under 200 ms" means 95 of every ___ requests answer in under 200 ms.
hint: A percentile is a share of what?

prompt: Why does the course recommend 4 processors for the virtual machine?
hint: Two programs share it during a load test.

choices.text: Multipass refuses to start a VM with fewer processors
choices.why: It starts with one; the lesson even names a smaller configuration.

choices.text: The load generator and the box office run side by side
choices.why: Right. With too few, the generator steals the application's time and the numbers describe the generator.

choices.text: Java needs exactly four processors before JMeter starts
choices.why: JMeter runs on two; it is just slower to start.

choices.text: Ubuntu 24.04 needs four to install
choices.why: Ubuntu installs on far less.

prompt: Which part of the course cannot happen inside the VM, and why?
hint: Think about what the VM does not have.

choices.text: The load tests, because the VM has no network at all
choices.why: The load tests run inside the VM against 127.0.0.1.

choices.text: The secret scan, because git is not installed there
choices.why: git is one of the base packages.

choices.text: The screen reader, because the VM has no desktop to run it on
choices.why: Right. NVDA, VoiceOver or Orca run on your own computer.

choices.text: Prometheus, because it needs a graphical browser
choices.why: Prometheus is a server; it installs in the VM from Ubuntu's archive.

prompt: Why does the base install the JDK rather than only the Java runtime?
hint: What does Gatling do before it runs a test?

choices.text: The Java runtime is not in Ubuntu's own archive
choices.why: openjdk-21-jre-headless is in the archive; it is just not enough.

choices.text: JMeter refuses to start on a runtime without the compiler
choices.why: JMeter runs on a runtime alone.

choices.text: Gatling compiles its tests first
choices.why: Right. Gatling's simulations are Java code compiled before the run.

choices.text: The JDK is a smaller download than the runtime
choices.why: It is larger; it carries the compiler too.

prompt: How many milliseconds does the box office's stand-in for the payment provider wait on every booking?
Match each booking request to the status the box office answers with.

pairs.left: a free seat of a show on sale
the same seat a second time
a body without the seat field

prompt: In the transcript, GET /shows/990 answered with "Server-Timing: db;dur=17.8, pay;dur=0.0, total;dur=18.3". What does that header tell a tester?

choices.text: That the client waited 18.3 ms in total, connection included
choices.why: It is the server's own measure; the client also pays for the connection and the transfer.

choices.text: That the query took almost all the server's time
choices.why: Right. 17.8 of 18.3 ms went to the query counting the show's bookings.

choices.text: That the payment provider is down and was skipped
choices.why: pay is 0.0 because a GET does not pay at all.

choices.text: That the 95th percentile is 18.3 ms
choices.why: One request has no percentile; it takes many.

prompt: Five identical requests to an idle box office took between 17 and 20 ms. A colleague proposes the requirement "GET /shows/{id} answers in 18 ms". What is wrong with it?
hint: What happens with a sixth request?

choices.text: Nothing, since 18 ms is inside the range the five requests showed
choices.why: The next request may take 19 or 30; a single figure has no statistic and no load.

choices.text: It names no statistic, so every request is a separate verdict
choices.why: Right. Requests spread even with no load; a requirement must say which statistic, at which load.

choices.text: 18 ms is too strict a target for any HTTP server
choices.why: The number is not the problem; what it is a number of is.

choices.text: Response times should be written in seconds
choices.why: The unit is fine; the missing parts are not.

prompt: curl -s prints nothing and echo $? prints 7. What happened?

choices.text: The server answered with an empty body and status 200
choices.why: An empty answer would exit 0; 7 means no answer at all.

choices.text: Nothing was listening on the port curl asked
choices.why: Right. The server is stopped, or the terminal is on a different machine.

choices.text: The request timed out after 7 seconds
choices.why: Exit codes are not durations; a timeout is 28.

choices.text: The server returned an error status such as 500
choices.why: Without -f, curl exits 0 on a 404 or a 500.
